summary: Says SSL version 3.0 is not sufficiently secure and must not be used. TLS 1.2, among its successors, is considerably more secure and capable. It updates backward-compatibility guidance in several RFCs so that implementations stop negotiating SSLv3.

plainLanguage.summary: An old lock was found to be easy to pick. This says stop using it and switch to newer, stronger locks.

subtitle: Why SSL version 3.0 is broken and must not be used, with replacements.

tldr.problem: SSL version 3.0, released in 1996, has accumulated a long series of cryptographic flaws that make it insecure. Despite being replaced by TLS 1.0 in 1999, many implementations have continued to negotiate it for backward compatibility.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC mandates that SSLv3 MUST NOT be used or negotiated, either from clients or servers. Any version of TLS (1.0 or higher) is considerably more secure and capable.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7568 updates RFC 5246 and related standards to explicitly prohibit SSLv3 fallback. It was itself updated by RFC 8996, which deprecated even earlier versions of TLS. SSLv3 is now Historical.

today: RFC 7568 prohibits use of SSLv3. It was updated by RFC 8996. SSLv3 is now effectively obsolete; modern implementations and browsers reject it entirely.

sections.title: Why SSLv3 Must Be Retired
sections.content:
SSL version 3.0 (SSLv3), first released in 1996, has been subject to a long series of attacks on both its key exchange mechanism and its encryption schemes. Despite being replaced by TLS 1.0 in 1999, and then TLS 1.1 (2002) and TLS 1.2 (2006), availability of these newer versions was not universal. Many TLS implementations permitted negotiation back to SSLv3 for backward compatibility with older systems.

SSLv3's predecessor, SSL version 2, was already prohibited. Now SSLv3 follows. Any version of TLS is more secure than SSLv3; the highest version available should be preferred.
sections.plainLanguage: SSLv3 is an old security lock from 1996. It has been broken by attackers many times. Even though better locks were invented in 1999, some systems kept accepting the old lock. Now everyone must stop using it.

sections.title: Record Layer Vulnerabilities
sections.content:
SSLv3's record layer uses Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) mode with non-deterministic padding, which trivially permits recovery of plaintext through the POODLE attack. The flaw is fundamental: SSLv3 uses a flawed MAC-then-encrypt construction that was later replaced in TLS versions using extensions (a feature added in TLS 1.0).

SSLv3 cannot be updated to fix this flaw in the same way because it does not support extensions. The stream ciphers defined in SSLv3 are also weak: of those defined, only RC4 is in widespread use, but RC4 exhibits serious biases and is no longer fit for use. This leaves SSLv3 with no suitable record protection mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: SSLv3's way of scrambling data (CBC mode) has a hole that lets attackers peek at the messages. The newer TLS versions fixed this, but SSLv3 cannot be fixed the same way.

sections.title: Key Exchange and Cryptographic Flaws
sections.content:
SSLv3's key exchange is vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks when renegotiation or session resumption are used. Each flaw has been fixed in TLS by means of extensions, but SSLv3 cannot be updated to correct these flaws.

SSLv3 also defines custom cryptographic constructions for the Pseudorandom Function (PRF), Hashed Message Authentication Code (HMAC), and digital signature primitives. These custom constructions lack the deep cryptographic scrutiny that standard constructions used by TLS have received. Critically, all SSLv3 primitives rely on SHA-1 and MD5, both considered weak and being replaced with stronger algorithms like SHA-256.
sections.plainLanguage: SSLv3 uses old, custom ways to mix up keys and verify messages that experts have found weak. Newer TLS uses standard methods that have been studied much more carefully.

sections.title: What Clients and Servers Must Do
sections.content:
Clients MUST NOT send a ClientHello with client_version set to {03,00}. Servers MUST NOT send a ServerHello with server_version set to {03,00}. Any party receiving a Hello message with protocol version {03,00} MUST respond with a protocol_version alert and close the connection.

Historically, TLS specifications did not specify what the record layer version number could contain when sending ClientHello. Servers MUST accept any value {03,XX} (including {03,00}) as the record layer version for ClientHello to maintain interoperability with clients, but they MUST NOT negotiate SSLv3 itself. This allows clients with legacy record layer version numbers to connect, but guarantees they will use a secure TLS version.
sections.plainLanguage: If a client or server tries to use SSLv3, the other side must say no and hang up. But servers still accept old-style messages that might claim to be SSLv3, as long as the actual conversation uses a newer, safer version.

sections.title: Why TLS Versions Are Better
sections.content:
SSLv3 is unable to take advantage of the many features added to recent TLS versions. TLS 1.0 introduced extensions, which allow the protocol to be extended without breaking compatibility. TLS 1.2 added Authenticated Encryption with Additional Data (AEAD) modes, Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) and Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) for stronger key exchange and signatures.

Later versions added stateless session tickets for session resumption without server-side state, DTLS as a datagram mode for UDP-based protocols, and Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation to let clients and servers agree on which application protocol to use (such as HTTP/2). SSLv3 can benefit from new cipher suites but cannot benefit from these modern cryptographic modes and features.
sections.plainLanguage: Newer TLS versions have many new features like AEAD encryption and elliptic curves. SSLv3 is so old it cannot even use these, so it is stuck with weak tools.

sections.title: Status and Deployment
sections.content:
RFC 7568 was published in June 2015 as a Standards Track RFC. It updates the backward-compatibility section of RFC 5246 and predecessors to prohibit SSLv3. The RFC was itself updated by RFC 8996, which deprecated TLS 1.0 and 1.1 as well.

By the time this RFC was published, major browsers and servers had already begun rejecting SSLv3. The POODLE attack, publicized in October 2014, accelerated deprecation. Today, SSLv3 support is rare in modern implementations and is blocked by major platforms and browsers.
sections.plainLanguage: This rule came out in 2015, right after attackers found a big hole in SSLv3. Since then, almost all software has stopped supporting it.
